newsitem.title: UK: Defecting Conservative MP blasts Britain's Major.
newsitem.headline: Defecting Conservative MP blasts Britain's Major.

text.p: A British member of parliament who quit the ruling Conservatives for the small anti-European Referendum Party launched a vicious attack on Sunday on Prime Minister John Major.
In a series of newspaper articles, Sir George Gardiner said he could no longer stand Major's "equivocation" over policy towards the European Union, particularly the proposed European single currency.

"We have witnessed an abdication of national leadership without parallel in the last 100 years of British political history," wrote Gardiner, whose defection gave the Referendum Party its first member of parliament.
Britain was trapped on "an escalator to a European super-state", he said.
Gardiner accused the ruling party of being intolerant and showing "a nasty Stalinist streak".
His defection, which in theory pushed Major's government even further into a minority in the House of Commons, was shrugged off by Conservative leaders.
"I think it is regrettable but I don't think it will have any great national impact," said Social Security Secretary Peter Lilley.
The Referendum Party is scoring only around two percent in opinion polls and few people expect it to win many seats in the general election due by May.
But Gardiner's defection once again underlined the bitter divisions over Europe within the the ranks of the Conservative Party.
The Conservatives have ruled Britain for the past 18 years but opinion polls suggest they face defeat at the general election.
Major has been fighting to hold the line on Europe after crafting a policy designed to keep his cabinet united.

The policy, hammered out in January, is that Britain is keeping its options open on the planned single currency but is unlikely to join because the government does not believe other states will meet the strict economic criteria for entry.

However, the government has been plagued by statements by cabinet ministers like Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell and Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind that appeared to conflict with the policy. The ministers issued hasty denials that they were at odds with Major.
So-called Eurosceptics like Gardiner, who oppose all moves towards further European integration, have forced Major to take a tough line against Europe during his six-year stint as prime minister.

Even Major's decision to fight a party leadership contest over the issue in July 1995, a battle he won, failed to silence the Eurosceptics, whose influence grew as the Conservatives' parliamentary position weakened.

Gardiner is the fourth member of parliament to quit the Conservatives in the past 18 months. Two Conservatives joined the minority Liberal Democrats and another went over to the main opposition Labour Party.
It theoretically puts Major's government into a minority of three. But he can hang on thanks to support from Northern Ireland's nine Ulster Unionist legislators.

Gardiner's decision to quit was seen as almost inevitable after his local Conservative association chose another candidate for the general election after sacking the 62 year-old for remarks likening Major to a ventriloquist's dummy.
But the viciousness of his attack made Major's task of closing the 18-point opinion poll gap behind Labour before the election even harder.
